svg.text: NYC's congestion pricing program lifted bus and subway ridership well beyond the priced zone itself,
using time-series foundation models to build counterfactual demand forecasts where no clean control
group exists -- one of the first rigorous post-implementation reads of the policy.
A new dynamic program computes provably tight worst-case (not just average-case) bus headway bounds
under any holding policy, validated on a real Nashville, TN route -- closing a long-standing gap
between average-case optimization and what riders actually experience as unreliability.
Tabular reinforcement learning matched Deep RL's metro-network-expansion performance on real Xi'an
and Amsterdam networks while using 18x fewer training episodes and 12x less carbon -- a direct
challenge to the assumption that bigger models always win at transit network design.

Donghang Li, Dingyi Zhuang, Yunlin Li, Chenan Shen, Nina Cao, Yunhan Zheng, Shenhao Wang, Jinhua Zhao
Using time-series foundation models to generate calibrated probabilistic counterfactual demand
forecasts, the study finds bus and subway ridership rose significantly relative to a no-policy
baseline, with transit gains spilling well beyond Manhattan's Congestion Relief Zone -- the most
consequential live US transit policy test of the decade, paired with a reusable evaluation method.

Agencies designing or revising fare policy should pilot agent-based, socioeconomically-stratified
simulation before launch -- equity and revenue effects are decoupled enough that intuition alone
is an unreliable guide to predicting outcomes.
Before adopting Deep RL for network design problems, benchmark a simpler tabular or search-based
baseline first -- for many real-world metro and bus network sizes it may already be competitive at
a fraction of the compute and carbon cost.
